items.question_text: Ship A and ship B are initially separated by a distance of 10 km along a north-south axis, with ship A positioned to the north of ship B. Ship A moves due west at a constant speed of 20 km/h, while ship B sails due north at a constant speed of 20 km/h. Determine the shortest distance between the two vessels and the time taken to reach this minimum separation.

solution.approach: Find the velocity of ship B relative to ship A, then find the shortest distance from A to the straight-line path that B follows relative to A.

steps.text: Set up coordinates with east and north as axes. Place B at the origin and A 10 km north of it, and write both velocities as vectors.
Find the velocity of B relative to A.
Find the position of B relative to A at t = 0.
steps.equation: r_BA(0) = B − A = (0, −10) km, that is, 10 km south of A

steps.text: Write the relative position as a function of time and minimize the squared distance from A (the origin of this relative frame).
Differentiate the squared distance and set it to zero to find the time of closest approach.
Substitute t = 0.25 h back to get the minimum distance.

final_answer.value: distance of closest approach = 5√2 km ≈ 7.07 km, reached after 0.25 h = 15 minutes

common_mistakes.text: Using the initial separation of 10 km directly as the closest approach, without accounting for the relative motion, misses that the two ships close in further before moving apart.
Adding the two speeds as 20 + 20 = 40 km/h for the relative speed instead of combining them as perpendicular vectors gives a wrong relative velocity of 40 km/h instead of 20√2 km/h.

items.question_text: A particle has velocity v = (2î) m/s at the start, and its acceleration varies with time t as a = (4tî + t²ĵ) m/s². Can the kinematic relation v = u + at be applied directly to find its velocity at a later time?

solution.approach: The formula v = u + at holds only for constant acceleration; since the acceleration here depends on time, velocity must be found by integrating it over time instead.

steps.text: The equation v = u + at is derived by integrating a constant acceleration over time, dv = a dt with a fixed.
steps.equation: v = u + at, valid only when a does not change with time

steps.text: Here the acceleration is a(t) = 4tî + t²ĵ, which changes with time, so v = u + at cannot be applied directly.
steps.equation: a(t) depends on t, so v(t) = u + ∫a(t) dt, not u + a(t)·t

steps.text: As a check, at t = 1 s the wrong formula gives v = u + a(1)×1 = (2,0) + (4,1) = (6,1) m/s, while correctly integrating gives v(1) = (4, 1/3) m/s, a different result.
steps.why_this_step: The mismatch confirms that plugging the instantaneous acceleration into v = u + at gives an incorrect velocity when acceleration is not constant.

final_answer.value: No. The equation v = u + at applies only for constant acceleration; here the acceleration depends on time, so velocity must be obtained by integrating a(t) with respect to time.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting the acceleration at an instant into v = u + at as if it were constant gives v = (6, 1) m/s at t = 1 s instead of the correct (4, 1/3) m/s.
